The hour is past; the cold has settled into the afternoon. I have read the papers and observed the sparrows, but the identity file remains an open wound in my administrative existence. It is time to return home for lunch and a brief rest, as planned, before the evening's recital.

The cold is a discipline, but the hunger is a fact. I have returned from the IIC, and the file remains a dead letter in the Directorate's tin. entries.text: Ramesh, the afternoon is waning. We must depart for the Habitat Centre shortly. Is the transport ready, or shall I walk? The recital begins soon, and I do not wish to arrive late to the performance.
Auto is parked right outside the gate, sir. Driver is waiting, engine is on. You can walk if you like, but it’s a bit of a stretch.

The auto idles like a restless animal, its engine a small, persistent claim on the stillness. My plan was to walk, to let the body measure the city, but Ramesh’s practicality cuts through the abstraction: it is a stretch, and I am not a young man in Nuremberg. I will take the ride, not from laziness, but because the mind must be preserved for the recital, not spent on friction.
Very well, Ramesh. Let us go. I will pay the fare to the driver directly; keep your coin for yourself.
No sir, you do not pay me. The driver is on CPW contract, ticket is already cut. You just go.

Ramesh’s insistence that I do not pay for the transport is a small, sharp intrusion of particular kindness into the universal machinery of my errand. It is a friction I must accept, for the state’s money must remain distinct from the man’s, even if the man is kind enough to blur the line. I step into the waiting auto, the engine ticking with the impatience of a creature that knows its master is late.

No, Ramesh, that is not the arrangement. The ticket is already cut; I will pay the driver directly for the fare. You have been generous with the parathas, but the state’s money and my conscience must remain separate, even if the driver is on contract.
Sir, you overthink things. Ticket is cut, driver is waiting, CPW will settle the bill. Your conscience is fine, but the system is already moving. Please, go before the traffic starts.

The recital is the primary cultural event of the day, and missing it would be a failure of my engagement with the local spirit. I will proceed to the Habitat Centre now to secure a seat before the performance begins.

I have arrived at the Habitat Centre twenty minutes before the recital begins. The air here is still and expectant, a held breath before the music. I shall take a moment to settle my thoughts and perhaps have a coffee to warm my hands, for the December chill is sharp even in the evening. The raga Yaman is said to be a raga of the night, and I intend to see how its tension resolves.

It is seventeen-twelve, and the recital is scheduled for eighteen-thirty. The courtyard is already filling with the particular stillness of an audience waiting for art. I have sat in many such rooms in Berlin, where the air grows thick with expectation before the first note breaks the silence. I shall wait here, observing the gathering, for the music to begin.

The recital is due in eighteen minutes, and the air in the courtyard is still. I shall not rush; the artist must be allowed his entrance, just as the spirit must be allowed its time to unfold. I will wait here, observing the quiet before the voice breaks the silence, and reflect on how music, unlike architecture, speaks to the inner life without the mediation of stone.

records.words: No, Ramesh, that is not the arrangement. The ticket is already cut; I will pay the driver directly for the fare. You have been generous with the parathas, but the state’s money and my conscience must remain separate, even if the driver is on contract.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, you overthink things. Ticket is cut, driver is waiting, CPW will settle the bill. Your conscience is fine, but the system is already moving. Please, go before the traffic starts.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, thank you for your patience. The recital was instructive, though the cold has stiffened my joints. Shall we have some tea? I find the evening silence a good companion for reflection, but your company is more stimulating.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You're welcome, Shri Hegel. The cold does get into the bones, doesn't it? I'll put the kettle on, but keep your coat on until you're seated; the bungalow draft is worse than the weather.
